Herodian’s -της workshop: accents & spelling contrasts

Type a Greek word (or make one up) and see (1) whether it matches Herodian’s suffix rules here, (2) a cited spelling or illustrative accent suggestion, and (3) the τραπεζίτης spelling fork (ι vs ει/η).

Mini-game: cited forms & toy accents

Herodian says several suffix-classes are βαρύνεται (“barytone”: accent not on the last syllable). Listed words retain their cited spelling; invented forms get an illustrative penult accent. It’s a simplification—meant for play.

1) Choose a suffix

Tip: try -οιτης, -ουτης, -υτης, or plain -της.

2) Give a stem

Join stem + suffix to restore a cited form, or try an illustrative accent for an invented form.

3) Generate

Quick reference (from this passage)

  • -οιτης (isosyllabic) → barytone (e.g. Δαμοίτης, Ἀνδροίτης).
  • -ουτης → barytone (e.g. Μαντούτης, τριακοντούτης).
  • Derivatives with long υ in -υτης → barytone (e.g. πρεσβύτης, Ἀρχύτης).
  • τραπεζίτης “banker/market-man” (from τράπεζα) vs τραπεζείτης “dog” (from τραπεζεύς), and τραπεζήτης in Ibycus (ει → η).

The verbal forms κωλυτής and μηνυτής are explicitly excluded from the long-υ derivative class. Unknown -υτης, -οιτης and plain -της forms need morphological information. This gadget is intentionally approximate: it doesn’t fully implement Ancient Greek accentuation or quantity; it just illustrates the idea of suffix-driven accent tendencies and a spelling fork.

original.english_translation:
Sinopean, Iopean, Akesitean, Pagasitean, Akmonitean, Abderitean, Gabalitean, Diolkitean, Memphitean, Naucratitean; εὐρείτης, βαθυρρείτης, ἀκαλαρείτης, “the one flowing quietly.” For among the Sicilians ἀκαλὸν means “quiet.” ἱερείτης, Samareitean, Atarneitean, Eleitean, Hagnoneitean, Maroneitean, Cauconeitean, Dicaearcheitean, Zeleitean, Oreitean, ἀλείτης, to which is set in opposition ἀλοίτης.

τραπεζίτης, in the sense of the man who works in the marketplace, is written with ι, for it is from τράπεζα; but in the sense of a dog, since it is derived from τραπεζεύς, it is written with the ει diphthong; and this is found in Ibycus, with the ει diphthong changed into η.

And all derivative forms that have long υ are barytone: πρεσβύτης, ἐλύτης, βασανύτης, ἁλκυονύτης, Ἀρχύτης, Πιδύτης, Αἰγύτης (an ethnic), as Pausanias has it, Κωβρύτης, Μωλύτης, Αἰπύτης, Πατρασύτης; whereas κωλυτής and μηνυτής are verbal and not derivative.

The isosyllabic forms in -οιτης are barytone: Δαμοίτης, Μενοίτης, Θυμοίτης, Ἀγροίτης, Φιλοίτης, Λαοίτης, Ἀνεμοίτης, Ὀροίτης, Ἀνδροίτης, Σακοίτης, ἀλοίτης, Ζιποίτης, king of Bithynia; and likewise the ethnic forms Βουτοίτης, from Βουτοΐτης, from the city Βουτὼ of Egypt; Σαβοΐτης / Σαβοίτης, the citizen of Sabu; Κυβοίτης, of Cybō.

The forms in -ουτης are barytone: Μαντούτης, by syncope from Μάντουα, just as Ζελείτης is from Ζέλεια; τριακοντούτης.

The forms in -της that have the penult ending in an unchangeable consonant, and that do not take σ in the genitive, are barytone, unless they are participial: ὑφάντης, ἀγύρτης, εὐφράντης, ὀξύντης, ἐγέρτης, ὀρίντης, αὐθέντης. Λαέρτης: there is also a place in Cilicia; Strabo book 14; and Alexander says “both a mountain and a city.” Σιβύρτης; Βερεκύντης.

Herodian · passage 1.235

One accent, two meanings

Explore the contrasts and limits of the compound-accent rule in this passage of Lentz’s reconstructed text.

Read the accent

A penult accent falls on the second-to-last syllable; an antepenult accent falls on the third-to-last.

The rule has limits

The active compounds discussed here normally have a penult accent, unless another rule prevents it. Try πρωτόπλοος and πολύλαλος for stated rules; try ἱππόδαμοι for an explicit difficulty.

Source: passage 1.235, including «ὄρνυσθ᾽ ἱππόδαμοι Τρῶες» (Il. Δ 509). This explorer covers listed examples, not general accent prediction. The next section on words in -υς begins in the same passage.

Herodian’s -της workshop: accents & spelling contrasts

Type a Greek word (or make one up) and see (1) whether it matches Herodian’s suffix rules here, (2) a cited spelling or illustrative accent suggestion, and (3) the τραπεζίτης spelling fork (ι vs ει/η).

Mini-game: cited forms & toy accents

Herodian says several suffix-classes are βαρύνεται (“barytone”: accent not on the last syllable). Listed words retain their cited spelling; invented forms get an illustrative penult accent. It’s a simplification—meant for play.

1) Choose a suffix

Tip: try -οιτης, -ουτης, -υτης, or plain -της.

2) Give a stem

Join stem + suffix to restore a cited form, or try an illustrative accent for an invented form.

3) Generate

Quick reference (from this passage)

  • -οιτης (isosyllabic) → barytone (e.g. Δαμοίτης, Ἀνδροίτης).
  • -ουτης → barytone (e.g. Μαντούτης, τριακοντούτης).
  • Derivatives with long υ in -υτης → barytone (e.g. πρεσβύτης, Ἀρχύτης).
  • τραπεζίτης “banker/market-man” (from τράπεζα) vs τραπεζείτης “dog” (from τραπεζεύς), and τραπεζήτης in Ibycus (ει → η).

The verbal forms κωλυτής and μηνυτής are explicitly excluded from the long-υ derivative class. Unknown -υτης, -οιτης and plain -της forms need morphological information. This gadget is intentionally approximate: it doesn’t fully implement Ancient Greek accentuation or quantity; it just illustrates the idea of suffix-driven accent tendencies and a spelling fork.

Offline, vanilla JS. Paste polytonic Greek freely.

original.english_translation:
Sinopean, Iopean, Akesitean, Pagasitean, Akmonitean, Abderitean, Gabalitean, Diolkitean, Memphitean, Naucratitean; εὐρείτης, βαθυρρείτης, ἀκαλαρείτης, “the one flowing quietly.” For among the Sicilians ἀκαλὸν means “quiet.” ἱερείτης, Samareitean, Atarneitean, Eleitean, Hagnoneitean, Maroneitean, Cauconeitean, Dicaearcheitean, Zeleitean, Oreitean, ἀλείτης, to which is set in opposition ἀλοίτης.

τραπεζίτης, in the sense of the man who works in the marketplace, is written with ι, for it is from τράπεζα; but in the sense of a dog, since it is derived from τραπεζεύς, it is written with the ει diphthong; and this is found in Ibycus, with the ει diphthong changed into η.

And all derivative forms that have long υ are barytone: πρεσβύτης, ἐλύτης, βασανύτης, ἁλκυονύτης, Ἀρχύτης, Πιδύτης, Αἰγύτης (an ethnic), as Pausanias has it, Κωβρύτης, Μωλύτης, Αἰπύτης, Πατρασύτης; whereas κωλυτής and μηνυτής are verbal and not derivative.

The isosyllabic forms in -οιτης are barytone: Δαμοίτης, Μενοίτης, Θυμοίτης, Ἀγροίτης, Φιλοίτης, Λαοίτης, Ἀνεμοίτης, Ὀροίτης, Ἀνδροίτης, Σακοίτης, ἀλοίτης, Ζιποίτης, king of Bithynia; and likewise the ethnic forms Βουτοίτης, from Βουτοΐτης, from the city Βουτὼ of Egypt; Σαβοΐτης / Σαβοίτης, the citizen of Sabu; Κυβοίτης, of Cybō.

The forms in -ουτης are barytone: Μαντούτης, by syncope from Μάντουα, just as Ζελείτης is from Ζέλεια; τριακοντούτης.

The forms in -της that have the penult ending in an unchangeable consonant, and that do not take σ in the genitive, are barytone, unless they are participial: ὑφάντης, ἀγύρτης, εὐφράντης, ὀξύντης, ἐγέρτης, ὀρίντης, αὐθέντης. Λαέρτης: there is also a place in Cilicia; Strabo book 14; and Alexander says “both a mountain and a city.” Σιβύρτης; Βερεκύντης.
